D1.label: SPACE WEATHER · ARCHIVED
facts: X-class flares and clouds (CMEs) from sunspot region 13664, 8–9 May 2024.
The clouds left 8 May and reached Earth and the Moon on 10 May.
Radiation storm level S1 to S2.

D2.label: RADIATION LIMITS
facts: NASA allows 250 mSv for one solar particle event and 600 mSv over a whole career.

D3.label: AIR LIMITS
facts: Each person breathes out about 350 litres of CO2 a day.
NASA's limit is 3 mmHg as a one-hour average.
D3.effect: AIR 40 = 3 mmHg. Amber at 3, red at 4.5
D3.source: NASA OCHMO CO2 and life support briefs

D4.label: PLANTS IN SPACE · ARCHIVED
facts: NASA's Veggie experiments grew lettuce on the space station.
The data is open in OSDR.
D4.effect: Grow choice sets the Ch. 4 harvest

D5.label: SHACKLETON · ARCHIVED
facts: The rim is lit about 70–90% of the time, and the floor never gets direct sunlight.

D6.label: LUNAR DUST · ARCHIVED
facts: Apollo crews found Moon dust clung to everything.
After Apollo 17, Harrison Schmitt said cabin dust gave him something like hay fever.
D6.effect: Dusty panels: POWER refill 7 instead of 10

D7.label: SPACE WEATHER · ARCHIVED
facts: X8.7 flare, 14 May 2024, the biggest of that storm, from the Sun's western edge.
Its cloud was aimed away from us.
D7.effect: If DONKI lists a particle event that week: storm strength 200. If not: drill only

happened: Launched into rain clouds.
Lightning hit the rocket twice and the power readings dropped out.
Controller John Aaron remembered a rare switch, "SCE to Aux", and Alan Bean flipped it.
Stuck in the lunar module after an explosion, the crew watched CO2 climb.
The spare canisters were square, and the sockets were round.
Engineers built an adapter from bags, cardboard, a sock and tape.
ML2.changed: Critical spares are designed to fit both spacecraft

happened: Planners packed the crew's days so tightly that they fell behind and made small mistakes.
After an honest talk about the workload, the schedule was eased and the work improved.
ML3.changed: Rest, meals and exercise are planned as part of the job

happened: Small errors added up and the lander came down kilometres past its target, toward boulders.
Armstrong flew by hand while Mission Control called "Sixty seconds", then "Thirty seconds" of fuel.
Boris Volynov was alone when his capsule re-entered facing the wrong way.
No one could help.
He stuck to procedure, landed hard, broke teeth, and flew again.
ML5.changed: Separation systems were redesigned; crews train for the "impossible"

happened: Armstrong and Scott thought the craft they had docked with was making them spin, so they undocked.
The spin got faster.
The real cause was a stuck thruster on their own capsule.
ML6.changed: Find the cause before the fix

happened: A grease gun leaked inside a spacewalker's tool bag.
While she cleaned it up, the bag drifted away.
ML7.changed: Tether and tool checks were tightened

happened: A supply ship steered by remote control hit the Spektr module.
The crew cut cables and sealed it off, and lost a big share of the station's power.
ML8.changed: Remote-docking tests stopped; power-loss plans got clearer

happened: The crew carried hundreds of envelopes that weren't on the approved list to the Moon, and some were sold.
None of them flew in space again.
An oxygen tank was dropped about 5 cm on the ground.
Later its heater switches failed because nobody had checked their voltage rating, and the wires were damaged.
In space, they sparked.
ML10.changed: Tanks redesigned; every part's paperwork checked

happened: Returning astronauts drop things, expecting them to float, and wobble for days.
Long missions weaken bones and muscles, so station crews exercise about 2 hours a day.
